input.question: Would a suction cup still have the ability to stick to a surface in a vacuum?
input.ground_truth: When a suction cup is pressed against a surface, it pushes out all of the air beneath it and creates a vacuum between the cup and the surface. This vacuum holds the suction cup tightly, and it will continue to do so until the pressure on the outside of the cup becomes lower than the pressure on the inside of the cup. (from [ehow](_URL_0_)) In a vacuum, the pressure outside will be the same as the pressure outside, so no, it will not stick to a surface.

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine you have a suction cup, like the kind you see on a bathroom scale or a toy that sticks to the wall.

Now, here’s how a suction cup works on Earth:  
When you press it onto something, the air tries to get out from under the cup. But because air is all around us, it can’t get out easily, so it pushes back and helps the cup stick.

But in a vacuum (which means there’s no air at all), when you put the suction cup down, there’s nothing to push back against it. There’s just empty space! So, the suction cup doesn’t have anything to stick to because there’s no air to hold it on.

So, in a vacuum, the suction cup **can’t stick** to the surface the way it does on Earth. It just floats there, because there’s nothing to push against.
